25078:
Isaac is the son of the promise, born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age after a quarter-century of waiting. His name, "he laughs," echoes both his parents' disbelieving laughter and Sarah's joy at his birth. He is the bridge between Abraham and Jacob: the covenant passes through him, God reaffirms Abraham's promises to him in the same words, and he is remembered in the formula "the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob."

Isaac is the quietest of the patriarchs. His defining early moment is passive: he is bound on Moriah as his father obeys God's command. As an adult he is shown praying for his barren wife, meditating in the field, farming successfully, and repeatedly yielding disputed wells rather than fighting for them. He also repeats his father's failure, calling Rebekah his sister to protect himself at Gerar.

In old age, blind and partial to Esau, Isaac is deceived by Rebekah and Jacob into giving the firstborn's blessing to Jacob. When the truth emerges he does not revoke it, recognizing that the blessing stands. Hebrews counts this blessing of Jacob and Esau as an act of faith concerning things to come (Heb 11:20).
25079: Isaac is born as promised (Gen 21:1-3), bound on Moriah (Gen 22:9), marries Rebekah at forty (Gen 25:20), prays for her and fathers twins at sixty (Gen 25:21-26), loves Esau for his game (Gen 25:28), receives God's renewed promise (Gen 26:2-5, Gen 26:24), calls Rebekah his sister (Gen 26:7), prospers and makes peace over wells (Gen 26:12-33), blesses Jacob in place of Esau (Gen 27), and dies at 180 (Gen 35:28-29). Paul treats him as the child of promise (Rom 9:7-10, Gal 4:28), and Hebrews says Abraham reasoned God could raise Isaac from the dead (Heb 11:17-19).
25080: The Akedah (binding) is central to Jewish theology of merit and martyrdom; some midrashim stress that Isaac was an adult who consented (Genesis Rabbah 56:8), and medieval liturgy recalls the "ashes of Isaac" as an appeal for mercy. Isaac is associated with the afternoon prayer (Minchah), from his meditating in the field (b. Berakhot 26b).
25081: Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain is a type of Christ carrying the cross, and the ram caught in the thicket a type of the substitutionary sacrifice (Melito of Sardis, *Peri Pascha* 69; Tertullian, *Against the Jews* 10).
25082: Isaac exemplifies the grace of election: he is the son of promise not of human effort (Rom 9:7-9), and his failures and passivity show that the covenant rests on God's faithfulness rather than the patriarchs' character.
25083: Ishaq is honored as a prophet and the son of Abraham through Sarah; Muslim interpreters have differed on whether the son of the sacrifice was Isaac or Ishmael, with the majority later favoring Ishmael.

25137:
Rebekah, granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor, enters Genesis at a well, where her energetic kindness to a stranger and his ten thirsty camels marks her as the answer to his prayer for Isaac's bride. Asked whether she will leave her family at once, she says simply, "I will go," echoing Abraham's own departure. She becomes Isaac's beloved wife and the second matriarch.

Like Sarah she is barren until Isaac prays, and when the twins struggle within her she takes the unusual step of inquiring of the LORD herself. The oracle that the older will serve the younger shapes the rest of her story. She loves Jacob, and when the aging Isaac prepares to bless Esau, she devises the deception that secures the blessing for Jacob, even saying the curse may fall on her.

The cost is high. Esau vows to kill his brother, and Rebekah sends Jacob away for what she thinks will be "a few days"; the text never records her seeing him again. Readers debate whether she acted in faith to fulfill God's word or in manipulation that God overruled, and the text itself passes no explicit verdict.
25138: Rebekah is the daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, and sister of Laban (Gen 24:15, Gen 24:29). She waters the camels (Gen 24:18-20), agrees to go (Gen 24:58), marries Isaac (Gen 24:67), inquires of the LORD and receives the oracle (Gen 25:22-23), loves Jacob (Gen 25:28), plans the deception (Gen 27:5-17), and sends Jacob away (Gen 27:42-45). Her burial at Machpelah is mentioned in Gen 49:31. Paul cites the oracle given to her as an example of God's purpose of election not depending on works (Rom 9:10-13).
25139: Rabbinic tradition generally portrays Rebekah positively, as a righteous woman who grew up among deceivers yet remained good, and as acting on prophetic knowledge when securing the blessing for Jacob (Genesis Rabbah 63:4, 67:9). Targum Onkelos renders her concern about the curse as a prophetic assurance.
25140: Patristic writers often read her actions as cooperating with divine providence and as a type of the Church (or of Mary) who prefers the younger people, the Gentiles; some, like Augustine, describe the deception as a mystery rather than a lie (*Against Lying* 10.24).
25141: Many Reformation and evangelical interpreters see faith in the oracle mixed with sinful means: God's purpose stood, but the deception brought family rupture and Rebekah's separation from Jacob. Calvin commends her faith while faulting her method.
25143: Some scholars highlight Rebekah as the most active of the matriarchs, who receives the oracle directly and drives the plot, and note that Genesis gives her more initiative than Isaac in nearly every scene.

25154: Rebekah is honored as one of the four matriarchs in Judaism and named in traditional Jewish blessings for daughters. Her question to God and the oracle she received became a key text in debates about election (Rom 9). The phrase "I will go" is often used in sermons on faith and calling.

25255:
Jacob, the younger twin of Esau, is the patriarch whose new name, Israel, becomes the name of the nation descended from his twelve sons. His story is the longest and most turbulent of the patriarchal cycles. Born grasping his brother's heel, he lives up to his name: he bargains Esau out of his birthright, deceives his blind father to obtain the blessing, and flees for his life.

God meets him in his flight. At Bethel he dreams of a stairway joining earth and heaven and hears Abraham's promises renewed to him. In Haran the deceiver is deceived: his uncle Laban substitutes Leah for Rachel, and Jacob labors twenty years, emerging with four wives, eleven sons, a daughter and great flocks. Returning home in fear of Esau, he wrestles through the night with a mysterious figure at the Jabbok, receives the name Israel, and limps into a reconciliation with his brother that he did not expect.

His later years are marked by grief: the violation of Dinah and his sons' revenge, Rachel's death in childbirth, and the apparent death of Joseph, his favorite. The family's rescue through Joseph brings Jacob to Egypt, where he blesses Pharaoh, adopts Joseph's sons, and speaks the oracles over his sons that anticipate the tribes' futures, including a ruler from Judah. Hebrews remembers him blessing Joseph's sons in faith while leaning on his staff (Heb 11:21).
25256: Genesis narrates Jacob's birth and early rivalry (Gen 25:19-34), the stolen blessing (Gen 27), Bethel (Gen 28:10-22), his years with Laban (Gen 29-31), Peniel and reconciliation with Esau (Gen 32-33), Shechem and Bethel (Gen 34-35), his grief over Joseph (Gen 37:31-35), the descent to Egypt (Gen 46-47), and his final blessings and death (Gen 48-50). He calls his own days "few and evil" (Gen 47:9). Hosea recalls that he strove with God and wept and sought favor (Hos 12:3-4). Malachi and Paul cite "Jacob I loved" (Mal 1:2, Rom 9:13). Jesus mentions Jacob among the patriarchs at the kingdom feast (Matt 8:11) and the woman at Sychar speaks of Jacob's well (John 4:5-12). Stephen recounts his descent and burial (Acts 7:12-16).
25257: Rabbinic tradition largely idealizes Jacob as the studious "dweller in tents" (Gen 25:27) and the most complete of the patriarchs, while Esau comes to symbolize Rome and its successors. The ladder is read as a vision of the rise and fall of empires (Leviticus Rabbah 29:2), and the wrestling figure as Esau's guardian angel (Genesis Rabbah 77:3). Jacob is associated with the evening prayer.
25258: Jacob's ladder is a type of Christ, the mediator between heaven and earth (John 1:51), and of the Virgin Mary in Orthodox hymnography. Fathers such as Hilary and Theodoret read the wrestler as the pre-incarnate Word. The struggle at the Jabbok is an image of persevering prayer.
25260: Jacob is a prime example of unconditional election: God chose him before birth apart from works (Rom 9:10-13), and his story shows divine grace persistently transforming a flawed man. Others in the Arminian tradition read Rom 9 here as about the roles of nations (Edom and Israel) in salvation history rather than individual eternal destiny.
